branch: Cyrillic Alphabet, Sound System, and Reading (Prerequisite Unit)
narrative: Teaches the 33-letter Cyrillic alphabet, the vowel/consonant inventory, hard/soft and voiced/voiceless consonants, word stress, vowel reduction, and the five intonation contours (ИК-1 to ИК-5). On completion the learner can read and pronounce any written Russian word aloud with correct stress-conditioned reduction and can hear the difference between a statement, a yes/no question, and a wh-question.

branch: The Bones of the Simple Sentence: Gender, "to be", and "to have"
narrative: Gives the three noun genders, the zero present-tense copula, and the locative-possessive у меня есть construction, so the learner can build and negate basic "X is Y" and "I have X" sentences before any case beyond the nominative. On completion the learner can identify gender from an ending, say what something is, and express possession and its absence.

branch: Case System Fundamentals: The First Three Cases
narrative: Introduces the concept of morphological case and teaches nominative, accusative, and prepositional in the singular. On completion the learner can say who does what to whom, where they are, and where they are going, with correct singular endings.

Teaches personal, possessive, demonstrative, interrogative, relative, reflexive, and negative pronouns and their declension. On completion the learner can substitute pronouns in all six cases and use свой correctly.

branch: The Rest of the Case System (Singular)
narrative: Completes the six-case singular with genitive, dative, and instrumental. On completion the learner can use all six cases in the singular for their primary functions.
Teaches long-form agreement and full declension, short forms, and comparative/superlative. On completion the learner can make any adjective agree in gender/number/case and form "bigger/the biggest".

branch: Plural Formation and the Plural Case System
narrative: Builds nominative plural and the plural endings of all six cases, including the notorious genitive plural. On completion the learner can handle nouns and modifiers in the plural throughout the case system.

branch: Verb Conjugation and the Tense System
narrative: Teaches the present tense of both conjugations, past tense, compound future, consonant mutations, and the main irregular/athematic verbs. On completion the learner can conjugate any regular verb and high-frequency irregulars in present, past, and imperfective future.

branch: Verbal Aspect: The Central Organizing Feature
narrative: The conceptual heart of the Russian verb: the imperfective/perfective opposition, aspect pairs, aspect across the tenses, and aspect in the imperative and infinitive. On completion the learner can select and form the correct aspect in past, future, imperative, and after phase/modal verbs.

Teaches the unidirectional/multidirectional imperfective pairs, then prefixed motion verbs. On completion the learner can distinguish "going (one way, now)" from "going (around/habitually)" and use prefixes for arriving, leaving, crossing, and dropping in.
Teaches cardinal and ordinal numerals and their irregular case government. On completion the learner can count, quantify nouns, tell time and dates, and decline numbers.

Teaches the four participles and the two gerunds — verb forms that compress a relative or adverbial clause into a word — plus the passive. Introduced for recognition at B1, required productively at B2. On completion the learner can recognize and form all four participles and both gerunds and convert between participial phrases and который-clauses.

branch: Complex Sentences, Mood, and Reported Speech
narrative: Builds the multi-clause sentence: subordinating conjunctions, the purpose clause with чтобы, the conditional/subjunctive with бы, and reported speech. On completion the learner can express cause, purpose, condition, concession, and time relations and report what others said.

branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register
narrative: Teaches how Russian's free morphology lets word order do the work English gives to articles and stress: the theme–rheme (given–new) principle, focus particles, and register/politeness (ты/вы, imperative softening). On completion the learner can order a sentence to put the right word in focus, use emphatic particles, and choose the appropriate politeness level.

branch: Sentence Skeleton & Verb Position (V2, the Satzklammer)
narrative: This unit installs the load-bearing wall of German syntax before any morphology: where the finite verb goes. On completion the learner can build statements, both question types, and imperatives with correct verb placement, and can already "bracket" a sentence around a second verbal element — the structural habit that every later tense, modal, and separable verb depends on.

branch: The Present Tense & the Verb Engine
narrative: With verb position fixed, this unit builds the verb forms that fill those slots. On completion the learner conjugates regular, stem-changing, and the key irregular verbs in the present, handles separable/inseparable prefixes inside the Satzklammer, and uses the present to express both current and (with a time word) future time.

This unit tackles the fact that every German noun carries grammatical gender and forms its plural somewhat unpredictably. On completion the learner can assign gender using reliable form/meaning cues, form the major plural types, capitalize nouns correctly, and read dictionary entries.

This is the conceptual heart of the course and its longest unit. On completion the learner understands what case is, can mark the subject/direct-object/indirect-object/possessor distinctions, and grasps that case, not word order, tracks "who does what to whom." Everything in Units 5–11 is an application of this unit.

This unit systematizes the words that precede nouns and carry case marking, splitting them into the two families whose behavior drives adjective endings in Unit 7. On completion the learner selects the right article/determiner form for any gender-case combination and understands the der-word/ein-word split.

This unit converts the case system into its pronoun paradigms. On completion the learner uses subject/object/indirect-object pronouns correctly, distinguishes formal/informal address, handles reflexive pronouns, and is prepared for relative pronouns in Unit 12.

This unit teaches the system English speakers fear most, but frames it as a logical consequence of Units 4–5: an attributive adjective's ending depends on whether the preceding determiner already shows the case/gender. On completion the learner declines adjectives in all three patterns and understands the "signal appears once" principle.

This unit adds the six modal verbs plus möchten, which combine with an infinitive to express ability, permission, obligation, and desire, reinforcing the Satzklammer. On completion the learner expresses modality in present and simple past and understands the modal word-order pattern.

This unit organizes prepositions by the case they force — the payoff of Unit 4. On completion the learner selects the correct case after fixed accusative, fixed dative, two-way, and genitive prepositions, and applies the motion/location rule to two-way prepositions.

This unit delivers the ability to narrate the past. On completion the learner forms and chooses between the spoken-past Perfekt and written-past Präteritum, selects haben vs sein as auxiliary, forms past participles of all verb classes, and sequences events with the Plusquamperfekt.

This unit adds the remaining indicative future tenses and the two grammar systems that express non-factual and agent-backgrounded meaning. On completion the learner forms Futur I (and receptively Futur II), builds and chooses between process- and state-passive, and uses Konjunktiv II for hypotheticals, wishes, and politeness.

branch: Clause Combination: Coordination, Subordination, Relative Clauses & Word Order
narrative: This capstone syntax unit lets the learner build complex sentences. On completion the learner joins clauses with the right connector type, produces verb-final subordinate clauses, forms relative clauses with correct gender/number/case pronouns, and orders middle-field elements by TeKaMoLo.

This unit consolidates the mid-level "connective tissue" that makes speech precise and cohesive. On completion the learner negates correctly (nicht vs kein), forms comparatives/superlatives, uses pronominal adverbs to refer to things behind prepositions, and links ideas with conjunctional adverbs.

branch: Register, Reported Speech & Foundational C1 Structures
narrative: This final unit crosses the B2/C1 threshold with the structures that separate an intermediate speaker from a genuinely advanced reader/writer of formal German. On completion the learner recognizes and produces Konjunktiv I for reported speech, reads extended participial attributes and nominal-style prose, and handles Funktionsverbgefüge — the backbone of journalistic, academic, and administrative German.

This unit builds the minimal machine for a French sentence: who does what, in what order, using the two most important verbs. On completion the learner can form simple affirmative statements, identify and name things, and say who someone is — the scaffolding every later unit hangs on.

Every French noun has a gender, and that gender radiates outward onto articles, adjectives, and some pronouns. This unit teaches the learner to assign and predict gender, form plurals, and understand why agreement is the connective tissue of the whole language.

French almost never lets a noun stand naked. This unit teaches the three article systems (definite, indefinite, partitive), the mandatory preposition-article contractions, and the demonstratives and possessives — giving the learner precise control over "the / a / some / this / my."

Adjectives are where agreement becomes audible and word order breaks the English habit. On completion the learner can describe people and things accurately, place adjectives correctly, and compare and rank them.

This is the engine room. On completion the learner can conjugate the three regular verb families plus the essential irregulars, handle reflexive verbs, use modals, and express the immediate future and recent past — enough to talk fluidly about routines, wants, and plans.
French negation is a two-part clamp around the verb, and the second part carries the meaning. On completion the learner can negate flexibly — not, never, nothing, nobody, no longer, only.

French offers three registers of question, and choosing among them is itself a sociolinguistic skill. On completion the learner can ask yes/no and information questions at every register from casual to formal.

branch: Object Pronouns, y/en, and Pronoun Ordering
narrative: This unit is the notorious clitic-cluster wall. On completion the learner can replace objects economically, use y and en, and order multiple pronouns correctly — the difference between halting and fluent French.

This is the aspectual heart of French. On completion the learner can narrate past events, distinguishing completed actions (passé composé) from background/ongoing description (imparfait), and can express "had done" (plus-que-parfait) — i.e., tell a real story with foreground and background.

branch: Future & Conditional, and the si-Clause System
narrative: This unit completes the tense grid and delivers hypothetical reasoning. On completion the learner can talk about the future, make polite requests, express wishes and hypotheses, and handle all three conditional (si) patterns.

The subjunctive is the documented "grammar plateau" that separates B1 from B2. On completion the learner can express necessity, desire, doubt, emotion, and subjective judgment — and stop paraphrasing around the mood.
This unit lets the learner combine short sentences into rich, connected ones. On completion they can build complex noun phrases and connect ideas the way native writers and speakers do.

branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative
narrative: This unit delivers the constructions that make French sound adult and precise. On completion the learner can shift focus with the passive, report what others said with correct tense-shifting, express simultaneity and manner with the gérondif, and get things done with causative faire.

Register is taught as a thread from day one and consolidated here. On completion the learner can choose tu/vous appropriately, shift between casual and formal negation/question forms, and recognize markers of spoken vs written French.

French carves up "time" with several non-interchangeable prepositions, and English's all-purpose "in"/"for" masks distinctions French treats as separate grammar. On completion the learner can correctly place a future point with dans, measure completion time with en, and state an ongoing or finished duration with depuis, pendant, and il y a (que).

This unit covers the small quantifier words — chaque/chacun, quelque(s), plusieurs, certain(e)s, and the shape-shifting tout — that let a learner say "each," "some," "several," and "all/everything" precisely instead of falling back on des or beaucoup de. On completion the learner can pick the right quantifier and get its agreement (or invariability) right, including tout's notorious adverbial exception.

For learners moving between French and Portuguese, this unit maps the true structural cognates and the real divergences, so that transfer helps rather than misleads. On completion the learner can leverage shared Romance architecture while sidestepping the specific traps.

Japanese doesn't use word order to show who's doing what — it uses small particles glued onto each word instead, which is why the verb can safely wait until the very end. This unit builds that particle-reading habit from the ground up, ending with topic-vs-subject and relative clauses, the two places beginners most often lose the thread.

One verb ending — the て form — is the hinge this whole unit turns on: it chains actions, builds requests, and feeds directly into the conditional and causative/passive forms covered later in the unit. Learn て form solidly and the rest of this unit is mostly reusing it in new contexts, not new material from scratch.

Politeness in Japanese isn't tone of voice — it's a grammatical choice built on the same verb-form instincts from the Verb forms unit, and i-adjectives conjugate on their own rules that don't map onto anything in English. This unit is short but changes how every sentence you build actually sounds to a listener.
